paper_metadata.title: SOCIOECONOMIC STATUS AND LIFESTYLE IN YOUNG ISCHAEMIC STROKE PATIENTS: A POSSIBLE RELATIONSHIP TO STROKE RECOVERY AND RISK OF RECURRENT EVENT

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The study uses a prospective, consecutive enrollment strategy within a defined age group (<50 years) at a Comprehensive Stroke Centre. Inclusion/exclusion criteria and baseline characteristics are well-defined, and the sample size (n=297) is substantial for this specific sub-population.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: While the 3-month outcome (MRS) seems well-captured, the long-term follow-up for RIS (median 25 months) lacks a clear flow diagram or description of the exact number of patients lost to follow-up. The authors admit that some follow-up was via phone calls to practitioners, which may introduce reporting bias.

risk_of_bias_assessment.label: Study Attrition Summary
risk_of_bias_assessment.prompt: Loss to follow-up (from baseline sample to study population analyzed) is not associated with key characteristics (i.e., the study data adequately represent the sample) sufficient to limit potential bias to the observed relationship between PF and outcome.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The study relies heavily on a self-evaluating questionnaire, which the authors acknowledge as a limitation. This introduces potential recall bias and social desirability bias, especially for lifestyle factors like alcohol and stress.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The study is primarily descriptive and uses univariable analyses (Chi-square, Mann-Whitney). The authors explicitly state the lack of power for logistic regression, meaning they did not adjust for key confounders like age or stroke severity (NIHSS) when evaluating the impact of SES/lifestyle.
